In mathematics, a '''superelliptic curve''' is an [[algebraic curve]] defined by an equation of the form
:<math>y^m = f(x),</math>
where <math>m \geq 2</math> is an integer and ''f'' is a [[polynomial]] of degree <math>d\geq 3</math> with coefficients in a field <math>k</math>; more precisely, it is the [[smooth scheme|smooth]] [[projective curve]] whose [[Algebraic function field|function field]] defined by this equation.
The case <math>m=2</math> and <math>d=3, 4</math> is an ''[[elliptic curve]]'', the case <math>m=2</math> and <math>d\ge 5</math> is a ''[[hyperelliptic curve]]'', and the case <math>m=3</math> and <math>d\geq 4</math> is an example of a ''[[trigonal curve]]''.

Some authors impose additional restrictions, for example, that the integer <math>m</math> should not be divisible by the [[characteristic (algebra)|characteristic]] of <math>k</math>, that the polynomial <math>f</math> should be [[square free]], that the integers ''m'' and ''d'' should be [[coprime]], or some combination of these.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Galbraith|first1=S.D.|last2=Paulhus|first2=S.M.|last3=Smart|first3=N.P.|title=Arithmetic on superelliptic curves|journal=[[Mathematics of Computation]]|volume=71|year=2002|pages=394–405|mr=1863009|doi=10.1090/S0025-5718-00-01297-7|doi-access=free}}</ref>

== Definition ==
More generally, a ''superelliptic curve'' is a cyclic [[branched covering]]
:<math>C \to \mathbb{P}^1</math>
of the projective line of degree <math>m \geq 2</math> coprime to the characteristic of the field of definition. The degree <math>m</math> of the covering map is also referred to as the degree of the curve. By ''cyclic covering'' we mean that the [[Galois group]] of the covering (i.e., the corresponding [[Function field of an algebraic variety|function field]] extension) is [[Cyclic group|cyclic]].

The fundamental theorem of [[Kummer theory]] implies {{Citation needed|date=February 2014}} that a superelliptic curve of degree <math>m</math> defined over a field <math>k</math> has an affine model given by an equation
:<math>y^m = f(x)</math>
for some polynomial <math>f \in k[x]</math> of degree <math>m</math> with each root having order <math>< m</math>, provided that <math>C</math> has a point defined over <math>k</math>, that is, if the set <math>C(k)</math> of <math>k</math>-rational points of <math>C</math> is not empty. For example, this is always the case when <math>k</math> is [[Algebraically closed field|algebraically closed]]. In particular, function field extension <math>k(C)/k(x)</math> is a [[Kummer extension]].

==Ramification==
Let <math>C: y^m = f(x)</math> be a superelliptic curve defined over an algebraically closed field <math>k</math>, and <math>B' \subset k</math> denote the set of roots of <math>f</math> in <math>k</math>. Define set
<math display="block">B = \begin{cases}
B' &\text{ if }m\text{ divides }\deg(f), \\
B'\cup\{\infty\} &\text{ otherwise.}
\end{cases}</math>
Then <math>B \subset \mathbb{P}^1(k)</math> is the set of branch points of the covering map <math>C \to \mathbb{P}^1</math> given by <math>x</math>.

For an affine branch point <math>\alpha \in B</math>, let <math>r_\alpha</math> denote the order of <math>\alpha</math> as a root of <math>f</math>. As before, we assume that <math>1 \leq r_\alpha < m</math>. Then
<math display="block">e_\alpha = \frac{m}{(m, r_\alpha)}</math>
is the ramification index <math>e(P_{\alpha, i})</math> at each of the <math>(m, r_\alpha)</math> ramification points <math>P_{\alpha, i}</math> of the curve lying over <math>\alpha \in \mathbb{A}^1(k) \subset \mathbb{P}^1(k)</math> (that is actually true for any <math>\alpha \in k</math>).

For the point at infinity, define integer <math>0 \leq r_\infty < m</math> as follows. If 
<math display="block">s = \min \{t \in \mathbb{Z} \mid mt \geq \deg(f) \},</math>
then <math>r_\infty = ms - \deg(f)</math>. Note that <math>(m, r_\infty) = (m, \deg(f))</math>. Then analogously to the other ramification points,
<math display="block">e_\infty = \frac{m}{(m, r_\infty)}</math>
is the ramification index <math>e(P_{\infty, i})</math> at the <math>(m, r_\infty)</math> points <math>P_{\infty, i}</math> that lie over <math>\infty</math>. In particular, the curve is unramified over infinity if and only if its degree <math>m</math> divides <math>\deg(f)</math>.

Curve <math>C</math> defined as above is connected precisely when <math>m</math> and <math>r_\alpha</math> are relatively prime (not necessarily pairwise), which is assumed to be the case.

==Genus==

By the [[Riemann-Hurwitz formula]], the genus of a superelliptic curve is given by
:<math>g = \frac12 \left( m (|B| - 2) - \sum_{\alpha \in B} (m, r_\alpha)\right) + 1.</math>

==Diophantine Problem==
The [[Diophantine problem]] of finding integer points on a superelliptic curve can be solved by a method similar to one used for the resolution of hyperelliptic equations: a [[Siegel identity]] is used to reduce to a [[Thue equation]].<ref>Shorey and Tijdeman (1986), Theorem 6.1</ref>

Stronger results are known. For a given polynomial ''f'' with rational coefficients and at least two distinct roots, the above equation has only finitely many integer solutions ''m'', ''x'', ''y'' with <math>m\geq 3, \vert y\vert\geq 2</math> and ''m'', ''x'', ''y'' are bounded by an effectively computable constant depending only on ''f''. Furthermore, the condition <math>m\geq 3</math> can be replaced by <math>m\geq 2</math> in the case ''f'' has at least three distinct roots.<ref>Shorey and Tijdeman (1986), Theorem 10.2</ref>

More generally, let <math>F(X, Y)</math> be a binary form such that <math>F(X, 1)</math> has at least two distinct roots and all of them belongs to a finite extension <math>k</math> of <math>\mathbb{Q}</math>, ''O'' be the ring of integers of <math>k</math>, ''S'' be the set of integers which are composed only of non-unit elements from a fixed set in ''O''. Moreover, take an ideal ''I'' from <math>k</math>. Then then equation
:<math>wz^m=F(x, y)</math>
with <math>w, y\in S, x, z\in O, m\geq 3</math>, and <math>(x, y)=I</math> implies that heights of ''w'', ''x'', ''y'', ''z'', and ''m'' are bounded by an effectively computable constant depending only on ''f'', <math>k</math>, and ''I''. Furthermore, the condition <math>m\geq 3</math> can be replaced by <math>m\geq 2</math> in the case <math>F(X, 1)</math> has at least three distinct roots.<ref>
Shorey and Tijdeman (1986), Theorems 10.6 and 10.7, see also {{cite conference | first1=T.N. | last1=Shorey | authorlink1=Tarlok Nath Shorey | first2=A. J. | last2=van der Poorten | authorlink2=Alfred van der Poorten | first3=R. | last3=Tijdeman | authorlink3=Robert Tijdeman  | first4=A. | last4=Schinzel | authorlink4=Andrzej Schinzel | title=Applications of the Gel'fond-Baker Method to Diophantine Equations | book-title= Transcendence Theory: Advances and Applications, Proceedings of a conference held in Cambridge in 1976 | editor-first1=A. | editor-last1=Baker | editor-link1=Alan Baker (mathematician) | editor-first2=D.W. | editor-last2=Masser | editor-link2=David Masser | publisher=[[Academic Press]] |publication-date=1977 | chapter=3 | pages=59--77}}</ref>
